purpose: Dexamethasone is used to reduce inflammation and calm down an overactive immune system. It can help treat a wide range of conditions including severe allergies, asthma, arthritis, skin conditions, certain cancers, and serious infections like COVID-19 or meningitis. Doctors also use it to prevent nausea after surgery or chemotherapy.
how_it_works: Think of inflammation as your body's alarm system going off too loudly. Dexamethasone works by turning down that alarm. It enters your cells and tells your immune system to stop producing the chemicals that cause swelling, redness, and pain. This powerful calming effect helps your body recover from illness or injury more comfortably.
common_side_effects: Increased appetite and weight gain, trouble sleeping, mood changes or feeling more emotional, increased blood sugar levels, upset stomach, mild swelling in your hands or feet, acne or skin changes, and feeling more energetic or restless than usual.
warnings: Do not stop taking this medication suddenly if you have been on it for more than a few days — your body needs time to adjust, so your doctor will slowly lower your dose. It can raise your blood sugar, so diabetics need to monitor levels closely. It can weaken your immune system, making it easier to get infections, so avoid people who are sick. Long-term use can weaken bones, so talk to your doctor about calcium and vitamin D. Always tell your doctor about all other medications you take.
typical_dosing: The dose varies widely depending on what condition is being treated. It can range from as low as 0.5 mg to as high as 40 mg per day, taken by mouth, injection, or eye drops. Your doctor will prescribe the right dose for your specific situation. It is usually taken with food to protect your stomach, and often in the morning to help reduce sleep problems.
